summary: Matter and atomic structure, the periodic table and element records, acids-bases-pH and common compound names, ores and alloys, carbon compounds, fuels, polymers, industrial processes and pollution. CGL asks 1-2 direct factual questions.

subtopics.title: Matter, separation methods and atomic structure
subtopics.concept:
### States and changes of matter
- Solid, liquid, gas; **plasma** is the 4th state (Sun, stars, lightning, neon signs); **Bose–Einstein condensate** is the 5th (predicted by S.N. Bose and Einstein).
- **Sublimation** — solid turns directly into vapour: **camphor, naphthalene balls, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice (solid CO₂)**.
- **Physical change** is reversible, with no new substance (melting ice, dissolving sugar). **Chemical change** makes a new substance (rusting, burning, curdling of milk, digestion, cooking).

### Mixtures and their separation
| Method | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Chromatography** | Separating dyes in ink, pigments, drugs in blood |
| **Distillation** | Liquids with widely different boiling points; pure water |
| **Fractional distillation** | Components of **petroleum** and of **liquefied air** |
| **Centrifugation** | **Cream from milk**, blood tests |
| **Sublimation** | Salt + camphor / ammonium chloride |
| **Crystallisation** | Pure salt from sea water, pure copper sulphate |
| **Separating funnel** | Immiscible liquids (oil + water) |

- **Colloids** show the **Tyndall effect** (scattering of a light beam) and **Brownian motion**. Examples: **milk** (emulsion — fat in water), **fog, clouds** (liquid in gas — aerosol), **smoke** (solid in gas), **butter** (water in fat).
- True solutions (sugar or salt in water) do not show the Tyndall effect.

### Structure of the atom
| Particle | Discovered by | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| **Electron** | **J.J. Thomson** (1897, cathode rays) | −1 |
| **Proton** | Canal rays — **E. Goldstein**; identified by **Rutherford** | +1 |
| **Neutron** | **James Chadwick** (1932) | 0 |
| **Nucleus** | **Rutherford** (gold-foil / α-scattering) | + |

- **Dalton** — atomic theory (atom indivisible). **Thomson** — 'plum pudding' model. **Rutherford** — nuclear model. **Bohr** — fixed orbits/energy levels.
- Atomic number (Z) = number of protons; mass number (A) = protons + neutrons.
- **Isotopes** — same Z, different A (¹H protium, ²H **deuterium**, ³H **tritium** — the radioactive one; C-12 and C-14). **Isobars** — same A, different Z (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca). **Isotones** — same number of neutrons.
- Shells hold at most **2n²** electrons: K = 2, L = 8, M = 18. Valence electrons decide chemical behaviour.
- **Avogadro number** = **6.022 × 10²³** particles per mole.
- Gas laws: **Boyle** — P ∝ 1/V (T constant); **Charles** — V ∝ T (P constant); **Avogadro** — equal volumes of gases at the same T and P have equal numbers of molecules.

tricks.title: Iso-words by the letter
tricks.body: Isot**o**pes — same atomic number (same **p**rotons, 'P for isoto-P-es'). Isob**a**rs — same **A** (mass number). Isoto**n**es — same **n**eutrons.

example.q: Deuterium and tritium are?
example.solution: Isotopes of hydrogen — same atomic number 1, different mass numbers.

tricks.title: Sublimation set: 'Camphor, Naphthalene, Iodine, Ammonium chloride, Dry ice' — 'CNIAD'
tricks.body: If an option is one of these, it is the sublimating substance.

mistakes: Calling milk a true solution — it is a colloid (emulsion).
Saying tritium is stable — it is the radioactive isotope of hydrogen.
Treating rusting or curdling as a physical change — both are chemical changes.
subtopics.notes:
### What is matter, and what forms does it take?
Anything that has mass and occupies space is **matter**. Besides the familiar **solid, liquid and gas**, science knows two more states: **plasma** (ionised gas — the Sun, stars, lightning, neon signs) and the **Bose–Einstein condensate** (matter cooled almost to absolute zero; predicted by S.N. Bose and Einstein).
Changes of state: melting, boiling, condensation, freezing, and **sublimation** — a solid passing straight to vapour. The sublimation set is a fixed exam list: **camphor, naphthalene balls, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice (solid CO₂)**.
A **physical change** changes only the form and is reversible (melting ice, dissolving sugar). A **chemical change** makes a new substance that cannot be brought back by simple means — burning, rusting, curdling of milk, cooking, digestion.

### Mixtures and how we separate them
A mixture keeps the properties of its parts; a compound does not. Separation method ↔ job:
| Method | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Chromatography** | Dyes in ink, pigments, drugs in blood |
| **Distillation** | Two liquids with very different boiling points (pure water from salt water) |
| **Fractional distillation** | Liquids boiling close together — **petroleum**, liquid air |
| **Centrifugation** | **Cream from milk**, blood/urine tests |
| **Sublimation** | Salt mixed with camphor or ammonium chloride |
| **Crystallisation** | Pure salt/copper sulphate crystals from a solution |
| **Separating funnel** | Immiscible liquids — oil and water |
| **Filtration / evaporation / magnetic separation** | Insoluble solid / dissolved solid / iron filings from sand |

### Solutions, suspensions, colloids
A **solution** (sugar in water) is clear and never settles. A **suspension** (muddy water) is cloudy and settles on standing. A **colloid** sits between the two: particles too small to see, big enough to **scatter a beam of light — the Tyndall effect** — and they jiggle constantly (**Brownian motion**). Colloid types to remember: **milk = emulsion** (liquid in liquid), **fog/clouds = aerosol** (liquid in gas), **smoke = solid in gas**, shaving cream = foam (gas in liquid), jelly = gel (liquid in solid).

### Inside the atom
- **Dalton** proposed that matter is made of indivisible atoms; **J.J. Thomson** found the **electron** and suggested a plum-pudding model; **Rutherford's gold-foil experiment** showed a tiny dense **nucleus**; **Bohr** added fixed **orbits (shells)**; **Chadwick** found the **neutron**.
- **Atomic number Z** = number of protons (the identity of the element). **Mass number A** = protons + neutrons.
- **Isotopes** — same Z, different A: hydrogen has **protium (¹H), deuterium (²H), tritium (³H)**; chlorine is ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl (average mass 35.5); **carbon-14** dates old remains. **Isobars** — same A, different Z (e.g. calcium-40 and argon-40).
- Electrons fill shells by the **2n² rule**: K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18; the outermost electrons are **valence electrons**; a full outer shell (octet) is stable.

### Counting particles — the mole
One **mole** of any substance holds **6.022 × 10²³ particles** (Avogadro's number) and weighs its molecular mass in grams. So **18 g of water = 1 mole**, and 36 g = 2 moles; 44 g of CO₂ = 1 mole. **Boyle's law**: at constant temperature, pressure × volume stays fixed (squeeze a gas, pressure rises). **Charles's law**: at constant pressure, volume grows in step with the kelvin temperature. Together: PV = nRT.

### Quick revision
- 5 states: solid, liquid, gas, **plasma**, Bose–Einstein condensate.
- Sublimation set: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice.
- Chromatography–dyes; fractional distillation–petroleum; centrifuge–cream; funnel–oil and water.
- Colloid = Tyndall + Brownian; milk = emulsion, fog = aerosol, smoke = solid in gas.
- Electron–Thomson, nucleus–Rutherford, orbits–Bohr, neutron–Chadwick.
- 1 mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles; 18 g water = 1 mol; PV = nRT.

patterns.name: Physical vs chemical change; sublimation and states
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a chemical change?', 'which sublimes?', 4th/5th state of matter, 'dry ice is…'.
patterns.logic:
1. New substance formed → chemical change (burning, rusting, curdling, cooking, digestion); only form changed → physical (melting, dissolving).
2. Sublimation list: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice — nothing else sublimes at room pressure.
3. Plasma = ionised gas in the Sun, lightning, neon signs; BEC = near absolute zero.
Why: the two change classes differ only in whether a NEW substance appears.

example.q: Burning of a candle involves —
example.solution: **Both** changes: melting of wax is physical, burning of the vapour is chemical.

patterns.name: Separation method ↔ mixture
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which method separates cream from milk / components of petroleum / dyes in ink?', match-the-column of methods and mixtures.
patterns.logic:
1. Match by property: different boiling points → distillation (close boiling points → fractional, e.g. petroleum); different densities → centrifugation (cream, blood); different solubility/movement → chromatography (dyes).
2. Immiscible liquids → separating funnel; dissolved solid → evaporation/crystallisation; magnetic material → magnetic separation; sublimable solid in a mixture → sublimation.
3. Cream-from-milk is ALWAYS centrifugation in exams.

example.q: The components of **petroleum** are separated by —
example.solution: **Fractional distillation** — the fractions boil only a few degrees apart, so a fractionating column is needed.

patterns.name: Colloids, Tyndall effect and Brownian motion
patterns.howToSpot: 'Milk is an example of…', 'scattering of light by colloidal particles is called…', which of these shows the Tyndall effect.
patterns.logic:
1. Classify by dispersed phase and medium: milk = liquid in liquid = **emulsion**; fog/cloud = liquid in gas = **aerosol**; smoke = solid in gas; shaving cream = foam; jelly = gel.
2. Light scattering by colloidal particles = **Tyndall effect**; zig-zag motion of colloidal particles = **Brownian motion**.
3. True solutions do NOT show the Tyndall effect; suspensions do but settle down.

example.q: **Fog** is a colloid in which —
example.solution: Water droplets (liquid) are dispersed in air (gas) — an **aerosol**.

patterns.name: Atomic models and discoverers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who proposed the plum-pudding / nuclear / planetary model?', 'which experiment discovered the nucleus?', order of models in history.
patterns.logic:
1. Timeline: Dalton (atoms indivisible) → Thomson (electron; plum pudding) → Rutherford (gold foil; nucleus) → Bohr (fixed orbits) → Chadwick (neutron).
2. Gold-foil: most alpha particles passed, few bounced → atom is mostly empty with a tiny dense positive nucleus.
3. Bohr's orbits are the K, L, M… shells filled by the 2n² rule (2, 8, 18…).

example.q: Rutherford's **gold-foil experiment** proved that —
example.solution: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged **nucleus** — most alpha particles passed straight through the foil.

patterns.name: Isotopes, isobars, atomic number and shells
patterns.howToSpot: 'Same atomic number but different mass number = ?' hydrogen isotopes, average mass of chlorine, electrons in a given shell for element X.
patterns.logic:
1. Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl → average 35.5).
2. Isobars: same A, different Z (Ca-40, Ar-40).
3. Shell filling 2n²: K = 2, L = 8, M = 18; for calcium (Z = 20) the arrangement is 2, 8, 8, 2.

example.q: How many electrons can the **M shell** hold at most?

patterns.name: Mole and gas-law numericals
patterns.howToSpot: Moles from a given mass, number of molecules, or a Boyle/Charles volume-pressure-temperature change.
patterns.logic:
1. Find molar mass first: H₂O = 18, CO₂ = 44. Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass.
2. Boyle: multiply each state's P and V, equate the two products.
3. Charles: convert temperatures to **kelvin** (add 273) before dividing.
Why: a mole is just a counting unit, and the gas laws are simple proportionalities.

example.q: A gas occupies **600 mL at 1 atm**. What pressure will squeeze it into **400 mL** at the same temperature?
example.solution: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 1 × 600 = P₂ × 400 → P₂ = **1.5 atm**.

subtopics.title: Periodic table, elements and record-holders
subtopics.concept:
### History of classification
| Scientist | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Döbereiner** | **Triads** (e.g. Li, Na, K) |
| **Newlands** | **Law of octaves** (every 8th element similar) |
| **Mendeleev** | Periodic table based on **atomic mass**; left gaps and predicted eka-aluminium (gallium), eka-silicon (germanium) |
| **Moseley** | **Modern periodic law** — properties depend on **atomic number** |

- The modern (long form) table has **18 groups** (vertical) and **7 periods** (horizontal); **118** named elements.
- **Group 1** — alkali metals (Li, Na, K…); **Group 2** — alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca…); **Group 17** — **halogens** (F, Cl, Br, I); **Group 18** — **noble gases** (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn).
- Across a period (left → right): atomic size **decreases**, metallic character decreases, electronegativity increases. Down a group: size **increases**, metallic character increases.
- **Fluorine** is the most electronegative element.

### Record-holders (static favourites)
| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Most abundant element in the universe | **Hydrogen** |
| Most abundant element in Earth's crust | **Oxygen** (then silicon) |
| Most abundant **metal** in Earth's crust | **Aluminium** (then iron) |
| Most abundant gas in the atmosphere | **Nitrogen** (about 78%), then oxygen (about 21%), then argon |
| Most abundant element in the human body | **Oxygen** (by mass) |
| Lightest element / lightest metal | **Hydrogen** / **Lithium** |
| Metal that is **liquid** at room temperature | **Mercury** (Bromine is the liquid **non-metal**) |
| Metal that melts in the palm | **Gallium** (about 30 °C) |
| Hardest natural substance | **Diamond** |
| Best conductor of electricity | **Silver** (then copper) |
| Most malleable and ductile metal | **Gold** |
| Metal with the highest melting point | **Tungsten** |
| Non-metal that conducts electricity | **Graphite** |
| Lustrous non-metal | **Iodine** |

### Noble gases and their uses
- **Helium** — balloons and airships (light, non-inflammable), breathing mix for deep-sea divers.
- **Neon** — advertising signs (orange-red glow). **Argon** — filled in **electric bulbs**. **Xenon** — flash lamps. **Radon** — radioactive.
- **Metalloids**: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium.

tricks.title: Crust order: 'OSAIC' — Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium, Iron, Calcium
tricks.body: So the most abundant element is O and the most abundant **metal** is Al.

example.q: Most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
example.solution: Aluminium.

tricks.title: Two liquids at room temperature
tricks.body: **Mercury** — metal; **Bromine** — non-metal. Gallium and caesium melt just above room temperature.

mistakes: Saying Mendeleev's table was based on atomic number — it used atomic mass; Moseley used atomic number.
Answering iron for the most abundant metal in the crust — it is aluminium.
Answering oxygen for the most abundant gas in air — it is nitrogen.
subtopics.notes:
### How the table grew
Chemists kept discovering elements, so they needed a map. **Döbereiner** noticed **triads** (Li–Na–K: the middle element's mass is the average of the other two). **Newlands** arranged elements by mass and found every 8th one similar — the **law of octaves**. **Mendeleev** made the real breakthrough: a table built on **atomic mass**, in which he left gaps and predicted unknown elements — his **eka-aluminium turned out to be gallium** and **eka-silicon, germanium**. Finally **H.G.J. Moseley** showed that properties depend on **atomic number**, not mass — the **modern periodic law** — and the modern table was born.

### Reading the modern table
The modern (long-form) table has **18 vertical groups** and **7 horizontal periods**; **118 elements** are named today. Elements in a group share outer-shell electrons (valency), so they behave alike.
| Region | Members |
|---|---|
| Group 1 | **Alkali metals** — Li, Na, K (very reactive, stored in kerosene) |
| Group 2 | **Alkaline earth metals** — Be, Mg, Ca |
| Groups 3–12 | **Transition metals** — Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au |
| Group 17 | **Halogens** — F, Cl, Br, I (salt-formers) |
| Group 18 | **Noble (inert) gases** — He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn |
| Two bottom rows | **Lanthanides** and **Actinides** (includes uranium) |

### Trends — the two directions
- **Across a period (left → right):** atomic size **decreases**, metallic character **decreases**, electronegativity (pull on electrons) **increases**. Sodium is a metal; chlorine at the far right is a non-metal.
- **Down a group (top → bottom):** atomic size **increases**, metallic character **increases**, so reactivity of metals grows (K is wilder than Na).
- **Fluorine** is the **most electronegative** element; **caesium** is the most electropositive (reactive) stable metal.

### Record-holders — the static-GK list
| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Most abundant element in the **universe** | Hydrogen |
| Most abundant element in **Earth's crust** | Oxygen (then silicon — 'OSAIC': O, Si, Al, Fe, Ca) |
| Most abundant **metal in the crust** | Aluminium (then iron) |
| Most abundant gas in the **atmosphere** | Nitrogen (≈ 78%) |
| Most abundant element in the **human body** | Oxygen (most abundant metal in body: calcium) |
| **Lightest** element / gas | Hydrogen |
| **Lightest metal** | Lithium |
| Only **liquid metal** at room temperature | Mercury (gallium melts in the palm, ~30 °C) |
| Only **liquid non-metal** | Bromine |
| **Hardest** natural substance | Diamond (an allotrope of carbon) |
| **Softest** mineral | Talc |
| Best **conductor** among metals | Silver (graphite conducts among non-metals) |
| Most **ductile and malleable** metal | Gold |
| **Highest melting point** metal | Tungsten (used as bulb filament) |
| **Densest** natural element | Osmium |
| **First man-made** element | Technetium |
| Non-metal that conducts electricity | Graphite |

### Symbols from Latin names
Several chemical symbols come from Latin: **Na** (natrium) sodium, **K** (kalium) potassium, **Fe** (ferrum) iron, **Cu** (cuprum) copper, **Ag** (argentum) silver, **Au** (aurum) gold, **Pb** (plumbum) lead, **Sn** (stannum) tin, **Hg** (hydrargyrum) mercury, **Sb** (stibium) antimony, **W** (wolfram) tungsten. Exams love these mismatch traps — sodium is NOT 'So'.

### Quick revision
- Döbereiner triads → Newlands octaves → Mendeleev (mass, gaps) → Moseley (atomic number).
- 18 groups, 7 periods, 118 elements; group 1 alkali, 2 alkaline earth, 17 halogens, 18 noble gases.
- Across period: size ↓, metal character ↓. Down group: size ↑, metal character ↑.
- Fluorine most electronegative; caesium most electropositive stable metal.
- Records: H–universe, O–crust, Al–crust metal, N–air, Ca–body metal; Li lightest metal; Hg liquid metal; Br liquid non-metal; Au most ductile; W highest melting point.

patterns.name: Element record-holders
patterns.howToSpot: 'Most abundant element/metal in the crust/body/universe', 'lightest metal', 'only liquid metal/non-metal', 'hardest natural substance', 'first man-made element'.
patterns.logic:
1. Abundance chain: H (universe) → O (crust; then Si, Al, Fe) → Al (crust metal; then Fe) → N (air 78%) → O (body; Ca is the body's top metal).
2. Oddities: Li lightest metal, Hg liquid metal, Br liquid non-metal, graphite conducts, Au most ductile, W highest melting point, technetium first man-made.
3. In 'odd one out' questions, check for these records first.

example.q: The most abundant **metal** in the Earth's crust is —
example.solution: **Aluminium** (about 8%), ahead of iron. Oxygen is the most abundant element overall.

patterns.name: Symbols from Latin names
patterns.howToSpot: A wrong-symbol pair (Na–sodium, K–potassium, Fe–iron, Ag–silver, Au–gold, Pb–lead) is given and the mistake must be found.
patterns.logic:
1. Memorise the Latin list: natrium–Na, kalium–K, ferrum–Fe, cuprum–Cu, argentum–Ag, aurum–Au, plumbum–Pb, stannum–Sn, hydrargyrum–Hg, stibium–Sb, wolfram–W.
2. In 'wrong symbol' questions the answer is almost always one of these eleven.
3. Others follow the English name (He, Ca, Zn…).

example.q:
Which symbol–element pair is **wrong**?
(a) Fe–Iron (b) Au–Gold (c) Ag–Silver (d) So–Sodium
example.solution: **(d)** — sodium's symbol is **Na** (Latin natrium), not 'So'.

patterns.name: History of classification
patterns.howToSpot: 'Law of octaves was given by…', 'Mendeleev's table was based on…', 'modern periodic law depends on…', 'eka-silicon is now called…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Chain: Döbereiner triads → Newlands octaves → Mendeleev (atomic mass, gaps, predictions) → Moseley (atomic number = modern law).
2. Mendeleev's predictions: eka-aluminium = **gallium**, eka-silicon = **germanium**.
3. Periods run by increasing atomic number today, not mass.

example.q: Mendeleev's **eka-silicon** is today's —
example.solution: **Germanium** (eka-aluminium became gallium).

patterns.name: Groups, periods and trends
patterns.howToSpot: 'Across a period atomic size…', 'down a group metallic character…', which group an element belongs to, number of groups/periods.
patterns.logic:
1. Fixed numbers: 18 groups (vertical), 7 periods (horizontal), 118 elements.
2. Across a period: size shrinks, metallic character falls, electronegativity rises; down a group: size grows, metallic character rises.
3. Most reactive non-metal sits at the top-right (F); most reactive metals at the bottom-left (Cs, Fr).

example.q: On moving **down a group**, the metallic character of elements —
example.solution: **Increases** — outer electrons get farther from the nucleus and are lost more easily (K is more reactive than Na).

patterns.name: Group families (alkali, halogens, noble gases)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which group contains halogens/noble gases?', 'why are group 18 gases inert?', 'which metal is stored in kerosene?'.
patterns.logic:
1. Group 1 alkali metals (Li, Na, K — soft, reactive, kerosene-stored); group 2 alkaline earth (Be, Mg, Ca).
2. Group 17 halogens (F, Cl, Br, I — form salts, F most electronegative).
3. Group 18 noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) have full outer shells, hence **inert**; He tops the list, Rn is radioactive.

example.q: Noble gases are chemically **inert** because —
example.solution: Their **outermost electron shells are complete**, so they neither give, take nor share electrons easily.

subtopics.title: Acids, bases, pH, common compounds and reactions
subtopics.concept:
### Acids, bases and indicators
| Indicator | In acid | In base |
|---|---|---|
| **Litmus** | Blue → **red** | Red → **blue** |
| **Phenolphthalein** | **Colourless** | **Pink** |
| **Methyl orange** | **Red** | **Yellow** |
| **Turmeric** | Yellow (no change) | **Reddish-brown** |

- **pH scale** (Sørensen): 0–14 at 25 °C. **< 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic.** pH = −log[H⁺]; each unit is a **10-fold** change in H⁺.
- Typical values: **gastric juice about 1.2–2** (HCl), lemon juice about 2–2.5, **pure water 7**, **human blood about 7.4** (slightly basic), milk of magnesia about 10.
- **Tooth decay** starts when mouth pH falls below about **5.5**. **Antacids** (milk of magnesia — Mg(OH)₂, baking soda) neutralise excess stomach acid.
- **Ant and bee stings** inject **formic (methanoic) acid** — rub baking soda. **Wasp stings** are alkaline — use vinegar.
- **Acid rain** has pH below about 5.6.

### Natural sources of acids
| Source | Acid |
|---|---|
| Vinegar | **Acetic** |
| Lemon, orange (citrus) | **Citric** |
| **Tamarind**, grapes | **Tartaric** |
| **Tomato**, spinach | **Oxalic** |
| **Curd**, sour milk | **Lactic** |
| Apple | **Malic** |
| **Ant sting, nettle** | **Formic** |
| Stomach | **Hydrochloric** |

### Common names of compounds
| Common name | Chemical name / formula |
|---|---|
| **Baking soda** | Sodium hydrogen carbonate, **NaHCO₃** |
| **Washing soda** | Sodium carbonate decahydrate, **Na₂CO₃·10H₂O** |
| **Bleaching powder** | Calcium oxychloride, **CaOCl₂** |
| **Plaster of Paris** | Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, **CaSO₄·½H₂O** |
| **Gypsum** | **CaSO₄·2H₂O** |
| Common salt | NaCl |
| **Quicklime** / **slaked lime** | **CaO** / **Ca(OH)₂** |
| Limestone, marble, chalk | **CaCO₃** |
| Caustic soda / caustic potash | NaOH / KOH |
| **Blue vitriol** | Copper sulphate, CuSO₄·5H₂O |
| **Green vitriol** | Ferrous sulphate, FeSO₄·7H₂O |
| **White vitriol** | Zinc sulphate, ZnSO₄·7H₂O |
| **Oil of vitriol** | Sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄ |
| **Muriatic acid** | Hydrochloric acid, HCl |
| **Epsom salt** | MgSO₄·7H₂O |
| **Potash alum** (fitkari) | K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O — water purification |
| **Hypo** | Sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃ — photography |
| **Laughing gas** | Nitrous oxide, **N₂O** |
| **Dry ice** | Solid CO₂ |
| **Heavy water** | D₂O — moderator in reactors |
| **Marsh gas** | Methane, CH₄ |
| **Lunar caustic** | Silver nitrate, AgNO₃ |
| Sal ammoniac | Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl |
| **Aqua regia** | Conc. HNO₃ + conc. HCl in **1 : 3** — dissolves gold and platinum |

### Types of reactions and everyday chemistry
- **Oxidation** = gain of oxygen / loss of electrons; **reduction** = the opposite. **Redox** reactions do both.
- **Rusting** of iron needs **both oxygen and water** (moisture); rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Prevention: painting, oiling, **galvanisation (zinc coating)**, alloying (stainless steel).
- **Rancidity** — oxidation of fats/oils; chips packets are flushed with **nitrogen** to prevent it.
- **Neutralisation**: acid + base → salt + water. **Displacement**: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one (iron nail turns brown in copper sulphate solution).
- **Hard water**: **temporary** hardness (bicarbonates of Ca and Mg) is removed by **boiling**; **permanent** hardness (chlorides and sulphates) by **washing soda** or ion exchange.
- **Plaster of Paris** sets into gypsum when mixed with water — used for **plasters on fractured bones** and statues.

tricks.title: Kitchen acid map: 'Vinegar-Acetic, Lemon-Citric, Tamarind-Tartaric, Tomato-Oxalic, Curd-Lactic, Apple-Malic, Ant-Formic'
tricks.body: Pairs that start alike help: **T**amarind–**T**artaric, **A**pple–m**A**lic (think 'mAlus', the apple genus), **F**ormica (Latin for ant)–**F**ormic.

example.q: Which acid is present in tomato?
example.solution: Oxalic acid.

tricks.title: Phenolphthalein goes 'Pink in Base'
tricks.body: '**P**henol → **P**ink' only in a base; in acid it stays colourless.

tricks.title: Vitriol colours by metal
tricks.body: **Blue** — copper (CuSO₄ crystals are blue), **Green** — iron (ferrous), **White** — zinc; **Oil** of vitriol — H₂SO₄.

mistakes: Swapping baking soda (NaHCO₃) and washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).
Writing aqua regia as 3 HNO₃ : 1 HCl — it is 1 HNO₃ : 3 HCl.
Thinking rust forms in dry air — it needs both oxygen and moisture.
subtopics.notes:
### Acids, bases and how we test them
An **acid** releases H⁺ ions in water (sour taste); a **base** releases OH⁻ ions (slippery feel) — a soluble base is an **alkali**. Indicators tell them apart:
| Indicator | In acid | In base |
|---|---|---|
| Litmus | Blue → **red** | Red → **blue** |
| Phenolphthalein | **Colourless** | **Pink** |
| Methyl orange | **Red** | **Yellow** |
| Turmeric | Yellow (no change) | **Reddish-brown** |
The **pH scale** (Sørensen) runs 0–14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic; each step is a **ten-fold** change. Key values: gastric juice ≈ 1–2 (HCl), lemon ≈ 2, pure water 7, **blood ≈ 7.4** (slightly basic), milk of magnesia ≈ 10. **Tooth decay begins below pH 5.5**; **acid rain** is below about 5.6. **Antacids** (milk of magnesia Mg(OH)₂) neutralise excess stomach acid; an **ant sting** injects **formic acid** — soothe it with baking soda.

### Where natural acids come from
Vinegar → **acetic**; lemon/orange → **citric**; **tamarind and grapes** → **tartaric**; **tomato and spinach** → **oxalic**; curd/sour milk → **lactic**; apple → **malic**; ant sting/nettle → **formic**; stomach → **hydrochloric**. This table is asked in nearly every paper.

### Common names and formulae — the core table
| Common name | Chemical name / formula |
|---|---|
| Baking soda | Sodium bicarbonate, **NaHCO₃** |
| Washing soda | Sodium carbonate, **Na₂CO₃·10H₂O** |
| Common salt | **NaCl** |
| Caustic soda | Sodium hydroxide, **NaOH** |
| Caustic potash | **KOH** |
| Bleaching powder | **Ca(OCl)Cl** (calcium oxychloride) |
| Plaster of Paris | Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, **CaSO₄·½H₂O** |
| Gypsum | **CaSO₄·2H₂O** |
| Quicklime | **CaO** |
| Limestone, marble, chalk | **CaCO₃** |
| Lime water | **Ca(OH)₂** |
| Milk of magnesia | **Mg(OH)₂** |
| Laughing gas | **N₂O** |
| Blue vitriol | **CuSO₄·5H₂O** |
| Green vitriol | **FeSO₄·7H₂O** |
| White vitriol | **ZnSO₄·7H₂O** |
| Oil of vitriol | **H₂SO₄** (sulphuric acid) |
| Alum (fitkari) | **KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O** |
| Heavy water | **D₂O** |
| Dry ice | Solid **CO₂** |
| Quartz, sand | **SiO₂** |

### Reactions and everyday chemistry
- **Neutralisation**: acid + base → salt + water. Acid + metal → salt + **H₂**; acid + carbonate → salt + water + **CO₂** (the gas turns **lime water milky** — the standard test for CO₂).
- **Chlor-alkali process**: electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution) gives **NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂**.
- **Baking soda** (NaHCO₃): mild, non-poisonous antacid; raises cakes and idli batter with CO₂; in soda acid fire extinguishers. **Washing soda** (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O): removes permanent hardness of water, cleans glass, makes borax and glass. **Bleaching powder** (Ca(OCl)Cl): disinfects drinking water, bleaches cotton.
- **Plaster of Paris**: made by heating gypsum to 100 °C; on adding water it sets back into hard gypsum — casts for fractures, statues, chalk.
- **Water of crystallisation**: CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; on heating it loses water and turns white, regaining colour on moistening.

### Quick revision
- pH: <7 acid, 7 neutral, >7 base; blood 7.4; tooth decay below 5.5; acid rain below 5.6.
- Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base. Ant sting = formic acid; tamarind = tartaric; tomato = oxalic.
- Baking soda NaHCO₃; washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; caustic soda NaOH; bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl.
- Plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O from gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O; lime water milky = CO₂ test.
- Vitriols: oil–H₂SO₄, blue–CuSO₄·5H₂O, green–FeSO₄·7H₂O, white–ZnSO₄.

patterns.name: Common name ↔ chemical name/formula
patterns.howToSpot: 'Baking soda is…', 'chemical name of washing soda / bleaching powder / plaster of Paris', 'which is CaO', formula asked for a common name.
patterns.logic:
1. Learn the core table by pairing: baking soda NaHCO₃ ↔ washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; quicklime CaO ↔ lime water Ca(OH)₂ ↔ limestone CaCO₃.
2. Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O loses water → plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O.
3. Vitriol family: oil of vitriol H₂SO₄; blue CuSO₄·5H₂O; green FeSO₄·7H₂O; white ZnSO₄.
Why: these names are fixed by tradition, so the only route is the pair-table.

example.q: The chemical formula of **baking soda** is —
example.solution: **NaHCO₃** (sodium bicarbonate). Washing soda is the stronger base Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.

patterns.name: Natural source → acid
patterns.howToSpot: 'Tamarind contains…', 'the acid in an ant sting is…', 'which acid is in curd/tomato/apple', match-the-column of foods and acids.
patterns.logic:
1. Kitchen map: vinegar–acetic, lemon–citric, tamarind+grapes–tartaric, tomato+spinach–oxalic, curd–lactic, apple–malic, ant sting+nettle–formic, stomach–HCl.
2. Trap pairs: tamarind is TARTARIC (not citric); tomato is OXALIC; apple is MALIC.
3. Base for an ant sting: baking soda (neutralises the acid).

example.q: The acid present in **tamarind** is —
example.solution: **Tartaric acid** (grapes also contain it). Lemon gives citric acid, curd lactic acid.

patterns.name: Indicators and pH values
patterns.howToSpot: 'Phenolphthalein turns pink in…', 'what colour does turmeric give with a base', pH of blood/tooth decay threshold, 'solution of pH 3 is…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Indicator colours: litmus blue→red in acid; phenolphthalein colourless in acid, PINK in base; methyl orange red in acid, yellow in base; turmeric reddish-brown in base.
2. pH: <7 acid, 7 neutral (pure water), >7 base; blood ≈ 7.4 (slightly basic); tooth enamel dissolves below pH 5.5.
3. Lower pH = stronger acid; each pH unit is a ten-fold change.

example.q: A solution has **pH = 3**; another has **pH = 5**. The first is —
example.solution: **100 times more acidic** — each unit below 7 multiplies H⁺ ten-fold (3 is two units below 5).

patterns.name: Salt chemistry and standard reactions
patterns.howToSpot: 'CO₂ turns lime water…', 'plaster of Paris is made from…', chlor-alkali products, what happens when water is added to quicklime.
patterns.logic:
1. Acid + carbonate → CO₂; CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ (lime water) → white CaCO₃ = milkiness (the CO₂ test).
2. Gypsum heated → plaster of Paris; water added → sets to gypsum again (fracture casts).
3. Chlor-alkali: electrolysis of brine → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂.
4. Quicklime + water → slaked lime, releasing much heat.

example.q: **Lime water turns milky** when CO₂ is passed through it because —
example.solution: Insoluble **calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)** forms — the standard test for carbon dioxide.

patterns.name: Uses of baking soda, washing soda, bleaching powder
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which chemical is used as an antacid / to remove hardness of water / to disinfect water', why cakes rise, composition of a soda-acid extinguisher.
patterns.logic:
1. Baking soda NaHCO₃: antacid, baking powder (CO₂ makes dough rise), fire extinguishers, mild alkali for stings.
2. Washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O: removes **permanent hardness**, glass and borax manufacture.
3. Bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl: sterilises drinking water, bleaches cotton, makes chloroform.
4. Match the job to the chemical; 'permanent hardness' always points to washing soda.

example.q: Permanent hardness of water is removed by adding —
example.solution: **Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O)**, which precipitates the calcium and magnesium ions.

patterns.name: Vitriols and water of crystallisation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Oil of vitriol is…', 'blue vitriol is…', why blue copper sulphate turns white on heating, formula with dot-water.
patterns.logic:
1. Vitriol set: oil of vitriol = H₂SO₄; blue vitriol = CuSO₄·5H₂O; green vitriol = FeSO₄·7H₂O; white vitriol = ZnSO₄·7H₂O.
2. The dot-water is **water of crystallisation**: heating drives it off (blue → white); moistening restores it.
3. Same idea: washing soda's 10H₂O; gypsum's 2H₂O.

example.q: On strong heating, **blue vitriol (CuSO₄·5H₂O)** turns —
example.solution: **White**, as it loses its five waters of crystallisation; adding water turns it blue again.

subtopics.title: Metals, ores, metallurgy and alloys
subtopics.concept:
### Ores
| Metal | Main ore(s) |
|---|---|
| **Aluminium** | **Bauxite** (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) |
| **Iron** | **Haematite** (Fe₂O₃), **magnetite** (Fe₃O₄), siderite |
| **Copper** | **Copper pyrites / chalcopyrite**, malachite, cuprite |
| **Zinc** | **Zinc blende** (ZnS), calamine |
| **Lead** | **Galena** (PbS) |
| **Mercury** | **Cinnabar** (HgS) |
| **Tin** | **Cassiterite** (SnO₂) |
| **Uranium** | **Pitchblende** |
| **Silver** | Argentite |
| **Sodium** | Rock salt |
| **Magnesium** | Magnesite, dolomite, carnallite |
| **Calcium** | Limestone, gypsum |

### Metallurgy steps
- **Concentration** — **froth flotation** for sulphide ores (pine oil used); magnetic separation; gravity separation.
- **Calcination** — heating **carbonate** ores in limited air; **roasting** — heating **sulphide** ores in excess air.
- **Reduction** — with carbon (iron in a **blast furnace**) or by electrolysis (aluminium — **Hall–Héroult** process; sodium, potassium).
- **Refining** — electrolytic refining (copper), with the impure metal as the anode.

### Reactivity series
**K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au**
- Metals above hydrogen give H₂ with dilute acids; **copper, silver and gold do not**.
- **Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene** (they react violently with air and water). **White phosphorus is stored under water** (it catches fire in air).
- Gold and platinum are **noble metals** — very unreactive.

### Alloys
| Alloy | Composition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Brass** | **Copper + Zinc** | Utensils, fittings |
| **Bronze** | **Copper + Tin** | Statues, medals, bells |
| **Bell metal** | Copper + Tin (higher tin) | Bells |
| **Gun metal** | Copper + Tin + Zinc | Gears, castings |
| **German silver** | Copper + Zinc + Nickel (**no silver**) | Utensils, decorative items |
| **Solder** | **Lead + Tin** | Joining electrical wires (low melting point) |
| **Stainless steel** | Iron + **Chromium** + Nickel + Carbon | Cutlery, utensils (does not rust) |
| **Duralumin** | Aluminium + Copper + Magnesium + Manganese | **Aircraft** bodies |
| **Magnalium** | Aluminium + Magnesium | Light instruments |
| **Nichrome** | Nickel + Chromium | Heater coils |
| **Amalgam** | **Any metal + Mercury** | Dental fillings (silver–tin amalgam) |

### Gold purity
- **24 carat = pure gold.** Purity % = (carat ÷ 24) × 100, so **22 carat ≈ 91.67%**, 18 carat = 75%.
- Jewellery gold is alloyed with **copper or silver** to make it harder.

tricks.title: Reactivity series: 'Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, I Like Her Calling Me Smart Goat'
Brass vs Bronze
tricks.body: **Br-a-ss** has **Z**inc (think 'brass band with **Z**ing'); **Bronze** has **T**in (bron**ze** medal — 'third'/tin). Both are copper-based.

example.q: Bronze is an alloy of?
example.solution: Copper and tin.

mistakes: Believing German silver contains silver — it is copper, zinc and nickel.
Naming haematite as an aluminium ore — it is iron; bauxite is aluminium.
Saying solder has a high melting point — its low melting point is the whole point.
subtopics.notes:
### Metals, non-metals and the exceptions
Metals are **lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors** of heat and electricity, and sonorous. Non-metals are mostly dull, brittle and insulating. The exceptions carry the marks: **mercury** is a liquid metal; **sodium and potassium** are soft metals cut with a knife; **graphite** (a non-metal) conducts electricity; **iodine** is a lustrous non-metal; **diamond**, the hardest natural substance, is a non-metal.

### Ore → metal
| Metal | Main ore(s) |
|---|---|
| **Aluminium** | **Bauxite** |
| **Iron** | **Haematite**, magnetite, siderite |
| **Copper** | Copper pyrites (chalcopyrite), malachite |
| **Zinc** | Zinc blende (ZnS), calamine |
| **Lead** | Galena (PbS) |
| **Mercury** | Cinnabar (HgS) |
| **Tin** | Cassiterite |
| **Uranium** | Pitchblende |
| **Sodium** | Rock salt |
| **Calcium** | Limestone, gypsum |

### Metallurgy — the four steps
1. **Concentration** of the ore: **froth flotation** for sulphide ores (powdered ore + pine oil + air — sulphide sticks to the froth); magnetic separation for magnetic ores; gravity separation.
2. **Conversion to oxide**: **calcination** = heat a **carbonate** ore in limited air; **roasting** = heat a **sulphide** ore in excess air. Memory hook: **C**alcination–**C**arbonate, roasting–sulphide.
3. **Reduction** to metal: carbon/CO in the **blast furnace** (iron); **electrolysis** for very reactive metals — aluminium (**Hall–Héroult process**), sodium, magnesium.
4. **Refining**: **electrolytic refining** — impure metal at the anode dissolves and pure metal deposits on the cathode (used for copper).

### Reactivity series and its uses
**K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.**
- Metals above hydrogen release **H₂** from dilute acids; **copper, silver, gold do not**.
- **Na and K are stored under kerosene** (they catch fire in moist air); Ca and Mg need care too.
- Metals below hydrogen occur **free in nature** (gold, platinum).
- A more reactive metal **displaces** a less reactive one from its salt solution (iron nail in copper sulphate turns the solution green).

### Corrosion and its prevention
**Rusting** needs **both air and moisture**; rust is hydrated iron oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O). Protection: **galvanisation** (coating with zinc — even the zinc's position above iron in the reactivity series lets it sacrifice itself), painting, greasing, electroplating, and alloying to **stainless steel**. Silver **tarnishes** black (Ag₂S with sulphur in air); copper grows a **green patina** (basic copper carbonate); aluminium protects itself with a thin oxide film (made thicker by **anodising**).

### Alloys — composition list
| Alloy | Composition | Use / note |
|---|---|---|
| **Brass** | Cu + **Zn** | Utensils, decor; not Cu+Sn |
| **Bronze** | Cu + **Sn** | Statues, bells |
| **Bell metal** | Cu + Sn (more Sn) | Bells, gongs |
| **Stainless steel** | Fe + Cr + Ni (+ C) | Cutlery; rust-free |
| **Duralumin** | Al + Cu (+ Mg, Mn) | Aircraft — light and strong |
| **Solder** | **Pb + Sn** | Joining wires; low melting point |
| **German silver** | Cu + Zn + Ni | Cutlery (no real silver) |
| **Nichrome** | Ni + Cr (+ Fe) | Heating coils — high resistance |
| **Invar** | Fe + Ni | Very low expansion — pendulums, tapes |
| **Amalgam** | Any metal + **mercury** | Dental fillings (except iron/platinum) |

Gold purity: **24 carat = pure**; 22 carat gold = 22/24 ≈ **91.6%** gold.

### Quick revision
- Calcination–carbonate, roasting–sulphide; froth flotation–sulphide ores; electrolysis–Al, Na.
- Al→bauxite, Fe→haematite, Hg→cinnabar, Zn→zinc blende, Pb→galena, Sn→cassiterite, U→pitchblende.
- K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au; Cu/Ag/Au give no H₂ with dilute acid.
- Brass Cu+Zn, bronze Cu+Sn, solder Pb+Sn, duralumin Al+Cu, stainless Fe+Cr+Ni, nichrome Ni+Cr.
- Rusting = air + moisture; galvanising = zinc coat; amalgam = metal + mercury; 24 carat pure.

patterns.name: Ore → metal matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Bauxite is the ore of…', 'cinnabar / galena / pitchblende is an ore of which metal', match-the-column of ores and metals.
patterns.logic:
1. Headline pairs: bauxite–aluminium, haematite–iron, cinnabar–mercury, galena–lead, zinc blende–zinc, cassiterite–tin, copper pyrites–copper, pitchblende–uranium, rock salt–sodium.
2. Trap: calamine is also zinc (with zinc blende); magnetite and siderite also iron.
3. In match-the-columns, fix the surest pair first (bauxite–Al) and chain the rest.
Why: each metal's name echoes in its ore except the classic traps, so recall by pair, not by logic.

example.q: **Cinnabar** is an ore of —
example.solution: **Mercury** (HgS). Heating cinnabar in air gives mercury vapour + SO₂ — an extraction by roasting alone.

patterns.name: Alloy → composition
patterns.howToSpot: 'Brass is an alloy of…', 'which alloy contains tin', 'stainless steel is made by adding…to iron', distinguish brass from bronze.
patterns.logic:
1. Copper family: brass = Cu + **Zn**; bronze = Cu + **Sn**; bell metal = Cu + Sn (tin-rich); german silver = Cu + Zn + Ni.
2. Iron family: stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni; invar = Fe + Ni.
3. Light metals: duralumin = Al + Cu; magnalium = Al + Mg; solder = Pb + Sn; nichrome = Ni + Cr; amalgam = metal + Hg.
4. The classic trap: brass is Zn, bronze is Sn.

example.q: **Brass** is an alloy of —
example.solution: **Copper and zinc.** Bronze is the copper–tin one; german silver is copper + zinc + nickel.

patterns.name: Metallurgy steps and processes
patterns.howToSpot: 'Roasting is used for … ores', 'calcination vs roasting', 'froth flotation separates…', 'which metal is extracted by electrolysis', 'Hall–Héroult process is for…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Concentration: froth flotation for **sulphide** ores (pine oil); gravity/magnetic separation.
2. Oxide conversion: **calcination = carbonate ore, limited air; roasting = sulphide ore, excess air**.
3. Reduction: carbon in the blast furnace (Fe); **electrolysis for Al, Na, Mg** (Hall–Héroult for aluminium).
4. Refining: electrolytic — impure anode, pure cathode (copper).

example.q: **Roasting** is done for —
example.solution: **Sulphide ores in excess air** — it converts them to oxides, driving off SO₂. Calcination is the carbonate-ore, limited-air version.

patterns.name: Reactivity series consequences
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which metal does not give H₂ with dilute acid', 'why is sodium stored in kerosene', 'which metal occurs free in nature', displacement-reaction questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Order: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
2. Above H → H₂ from dilute acids; Cu/Ag/Au do not react so.
3. Top metals (K, Na, Ca) catch fire in moist air → stored under kerosene; bottom metals (Au, Pt) occur free.
4. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

example.q: Which metal will **NOT** liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
example.solution: **Copper** — it lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series (so do silver, gold, mercury).

patterns.name: Corrosion and its prevention
patterns.howToSpot: 'Rusting requires…', 'galvanisation is coating iron with…', 'green coating on copper / black coating on silver', 'anodising is done on…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Rusting needs **both air and moisture**; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide.
2. Prevention: galvanisation (zinc coat), painting/oiling, electroplating, anodising (thicker oxide on aluminium), alloying (stainless steel).
3. Colour clues: iron–red-brown rust; copper–green basic carbonate; silver–black Ag₂S tarnish.

example.q: A **green coating** slowly appears on a copper vessel left in damp air. It is —
example.solution: **Basic copper carbonate** — copper reacts slowly with moist air (O₂, H₂O and CO₂). Silver instead turns black with silver sulphide.

patterns.name: Metal/non-metal properties and exceptions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which metal is liquid / soft / stored in kerosene', 'which non-metal conducts electricity', 'most ductile metal', carat-purity of gold.
patterns.logic:
1. Exceptions: Hg liquid metal; Na, K soft metals; graphite conducts; iodine lustrous; diamond hard but non-metal.
2. Best conductor among metals – silver; most ductile/malleable – gold; highest melting point – tungsten.
3. Purity: 24 carat pure; 22 carat ≈ 91.6%; carat also = 200 mg for gems.

example.q: Which **non-metal** conducts electricity?
example.solution: **Graphite** — free electrons between its carbon layers carry current, so it serves as electrodes.

subtopics.title: Carbon compounds, fuels, polymers, industry and pollution
subtopics.concept:
### Carbon and its compounds
- Carbon forms long chains and rings (**catenation**) and has valency **4** (tetravalency).
- **Allotropes**: **diamond** (hardest, bad conductor, each C bonded to 4), **graphite** (soft, layered, **conducts electricity** — pencil 'lead', lubricant, electrodes), **fullerene** (C₆₀ buckminsterfullerene), **graphene** (single layer of graphite).
- Hydrocarbons: **alkanes** single bonds (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, saturated), **alkenes** double bond (CₙH₂ₙ), **alkynes** triple bond (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
- **Methanol** is poisonous (can cause blindness); **ethanol** is the alcohol in drinks and is blended with petrol. **Vinegar** is about 5–8% acetic acid. **Esters** have a fruity smell.
- **Soap** = sodium or potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids, made by **saponification** (fat + NaOH). Soap forms **scum** in hard water; **detergents** work in hard water too.
- **Hydrogenation** of vegetable oil with a **nickel catalyst** gives vanaspati ghee.

### Fuels
| Fuel | Main component |
|---|---|
| **CNG** | **Methane** |
| **LPG** | **Butane** (with propane); **ethyl mercaptan** is added for smell to detect leaks |
| **Biogas / gobar gas** | **Methane** (plus CO₂) |
| **Oxy-acetylene flame** | **Acetylene (ethyne)** — welding and cutting |
| Water gas | CO + H₂ |
| Producer gas | CO + N₂ |

- **Hydrogen** has the highest calorific value by mass. **Octane number** rates petrol; **cetane number** rates diesel.
- Coal by carbon content: **anthracite > bituminous > lignite > peat**.
- **Ethylene (ethene)** is used for artificial **ripening** of fruits (calcium carbide, which releases acetylene, is banned for this).

### Polymers
| Polymer | Monomer / note |
|---|---|
| **Polythene** | Ethene |
| **PVC** | Vinyl chloride — pipes |
| **Teflon** | **Tetrafluoroethylene** — **non-stick cookware** |
| **Bakelite** | **Phenol + formaldehyde** — **thermosetting**, electrical switches |
| **Nylon** | First fully synthetic fibre |
| **Natural rubber** | **Isoprene** (polyisoprene) |
| **Rayon** | 'Artificial silk' from **cellulose** |
| **Melamine** | Thermosetting — crockery |

- **Vulcanisation** — heating rubber with **sulphur** (Charles Goodyear) to make it hard and elastic.
- **Thermoplastics** (polythene, PVC) soften on heating; **thermosetting plastics** (Bakelite, melamine) do not.

### Industrial processes
| Process | Product | Catalyst |
|---|---|---|
| **Haber** | **Ammonia** | **Iron** |
| **Contact** | **Sulphuric acid** | **Vanadium pentoxide** (V₂O₅) |
| **Ostwald** | **Nitric acid** | Platinum |
| **Solvay** | **Sodium carbonate** | — |
| **Chlor-alkali** | NaOH, Cl₂, H₂ (electrolysis of brine) | — |

- **Glass** = silica (sand) + sodium carbonate + limestone, fused; **borosilicate (Pyrex)** resists heat; cobalt oxide gives blue glass.
- **Portland cement** (Joseph Aspdin); **gypsum** is added to slow its setting.

### Pollution and poisons
| Substance | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SO₂, NO₂** | **Acid rain** (damage to the Taj Mahal — 'marble cancer') |
| **CFCs** | **Ozone layer depletion** |
| CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour | **Greenhouse effect** |
| **Carbon monoxide** | Binds haemoglobin (carboxyhaemoglobin) — suffocation |
| **Methyl isocyanate (MIC)** | **Bhopal gas tragedy, 1984** |
| **Mercury** | **Minamata disease** (Japan) |
| **Cadmium** | **Itai-itai disease** (Japan) |
| **Arsenic** | Black-foot disease; groundwater contamination |
| **Excess fluoride** | **Fluorosis** (teeth and bones) |
| **Nitrate** in water | **Blue baby syndrome** |
| **Lead** | Plumbism (lead poisoning) |

tricks.title: Process → product: 'Haber-Ammonia, Contact-Sulphuric, Ostwald-Nitric, Solvay-Soda'
tricks.body: Pair the catalysts too: Haber — **Fe**, Contact — **V₂O₅**, Ostwald — **Pt**.

example.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process?
example.solution: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅).

mistakes: Saying LPG is mainly methane — LPG is mainly butane; CNG and biogas are mainly methane.
Calling Bakelite a thermoplastic — it is thermosetting.
Naming phosgene for the Bhopal tragedy — the gas was methyl isocyanate.
subtopics.notes:
### Carbon — the backbone chemical
Carbon bonds to itself in long chains and rings (**catenation**) and always shows valency **4 (tetravalency)** — together these give it millions of compounds, the field of organic chemistry. Its **allotropes**: **diamond** (hardest natural substance, does not conduct, each C bonded to 4 others), **graphite** (soft, slippery, **conducts electricity** — pencil 'lead', electrodes, lubricant), **fullerene (C₆₀)** and **graphene** (one-atom-thick sheet).
Hydrocarbons: **alkanes** — single bonds, saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (methane CH₄, ethane); **alkenes** — one double bond, CₙH₂ₙ (ethene); **alkynes** — one triple bond, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne = acetylene).

### Fuels — what burns in what
| Fuel | Main component |
|---|---|
| **CNG** | **Methane** |
| **LPG** | **Butane** (+ propane); **ethyl mercaptan** added for smell |
| **Biogas (gobar gas)** | **Methane** (+ CO₂) |
| **Oxy-acetylene flame** | **Ethyne (acetylene)** — welding/cutting (~3000 °C) |
| Water gas | CO + H₂ |
| Producer gas | CO + N₂ |
Coal grades rise with carbon: peat → lignite → bituminous → **anthracite** (best). Petroleum ('black gold') is separated by **fractional distillation** into refinery gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil and bitumen (road tar, residue).

### Everyday carbon compounds
- **Methanol (wood spirit)** is poisonous — even small doses cause blindness; **ethanol** is drinkable alcohol, blended into petrol.
- **Vinegar** = 5–8% acetic acid. **Esters** (acid + alcohol) give fruits their smell.
- **Soap** = sodium/potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, made by **saponification** (fat + NaOH). In hard water soap forms useless **scum**; **detergents** work even in hard water.
- **Hydrogenation**: vegetable oil + H₂ with a **nickel catalyst** → vanaspati ghee (solid fat).

### Industrial processes — name ↔ product
| Process | Product |
|---|---|
| **Haber** | **Ammonia** (N₂ + 3H₂, iron catalyst) |
| **Contact** | **Sulphuric acid** (V₂O₅ catalyst) |
| **Ostwald** | **Nitric acid** (from ammonia, Pt catalyst) |
| **Solvay** | **Sodium carbonate** (washing soda) |
| **Bosch** | Hydrogen (from water gas) |

### Polymers and fibres
Polymers are giant molecules of repeating units. **Natural**: cotton (cellulose), silk and wool (proteins), starch, natural rubber. **Vulcanisation** (Charles Goodyear, 1839) heats rubber with **sulphur** — tyres get strength and elasticity. **Synthetic**: **polythene** (from ethene — bags), **PVC** (pipes, insulation), **Teflon/PTFE** (non-stick pans), **nylon** (first fully synthetic fibre, 1935 — ropes, parachutes), **bakelite** (first plastic, hard, thermosetting — switch boards), **rayon** ('artificial silk', made from wood cellulose).

### Pollution — pollutant ↔ effect
- **Carbon monoxide (CO)** binds haemoglobin ~200 times more strongly than O₂ → suffocation deaths from geysers and coal stoves.
- **SO₂ and NOₓ** → **acid rain**; **SO₂** was the killer of the London smog (1952).
- **Mercury** → **Minamata disease**; **cadmium** → **itai-itai disease** (both Japan, 1950s–60s).
- **CFCs** (old fridge/aerosol gases) ate the **ozone layer** — phased out by the **Montreal Protocol (1987)**; the ozone layer lies in the **stratosphere**.
- **Greenhouse gases** (CO₂, CH₄, water vapour) drive global warming; the **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** and **Paris Agreement (2015)** target emissions. The **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)** was **methyl isocyanate (MIC)**.

### Quick revision
- CNG/biogas–methane; LPG–butane (smelly ethyl mercaptan); welding–acetylene; anthracite–best coal.
- Haber–NH₃, Contact–H₂SO₄, Ostwald–HNO₃, Solvay–Na₂CO₃.
- Nylon first synthetic fibre; bakelite first plastic; vulcanisation = rubber + sulphur; Teflon non-stick.
- Methanol poison, ethanol safe-ish; soap scums in hard water, detergent does not; hydrogenation uses nickel.
- CO–haemoglobin poison; Minamata–Hg; itai-itai–Cd; CFC–ozone (Montreal 1987); Bhopal–MIC 1984.

patterns.name: Fuel ↔ main component
patterns.howToSpot: 'CNG is mainly…', 'LPG contains…', 'why does LPG smell', 'which gas is used in welding', 'best variety of coal'.
patterns.logic:
1. Gas family: CNG and biogas = **methane**; LPG = **butane** (+ propane); welding = **acetylene (ethyne)** with oxygen.
2. LPG leaks are smellable because **ethyl mercaptan** is added — the gas itself is odourless.
3. Coal ranking by carbon: peat < lignite < bituminous < **anthracite**; petroleum splits by fractional distillation (bitumen last).
Why: each fuel is a named hydrocarbon, so the answer is recall plus the one-line use.

example.q: The gas used with oxygen in a **welding torch** is —
example.solution: **Acetylene (ethyne)** — its oxy-acetylene flame reaches about 3000 °C and cuts steel.

patterns.name: Industrial process ↔ product
patterns.howToSpot: 'Haber process gives…', 'sulphuric acid is made by the … process', 'Ostwald process produces…', match-the-column of processes and chemicals.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the four: **Haber → ammonia; Contact → sulphuric acid; Ostwald → nitric acid; Solvay → sodium carbonate**.
2. Catalyst tags: Haber–iron, Contact–V₂O₅, Ostwald–platinum.
3. In match-the-columns, anchor on ammonia (Haber) — the rest fall into place by elimination.

example.q: The **Contact process** manufactures —
example.solution: **Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)** — SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ over a V₂O₅ catalyst, then absorbed in water.

patterns.name: Polymers, plastics and fibres
patterns.howToSpot: 'First synthetic fibre / first plastic', 'Teflon is used for…', 'vulcanisation of rubber is done with…', 'rayon is called artificial…', natural vs synthetic classification.
patterns.logic:
1. Records: **nylon = first fully synthetic fibre; bakelite = first plastic (thermosetting); rayon = artificial silk from cellulose**.
2. Uses: polythene–bags, PVC–pipes, Teflon–non-stick, nylon–ropes and parachutes.
3. Vulcanisation = natural rubber + **sulphur** (Goodyear) → tyres.
4. Natural fibres: cotton–cellulose; silk/wool–protein; synthetic: nylon, polyester, acrylic.

example.q: **Vulcanised rubber** is made by heating natural rubber with —
example.solution: **Sulphur** — cross-links form between chains, making the rubber strong, elastic and heat-resistant (tyres).

patterns.name: Allotropes and hydrocarbon families
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which allotrope of carbon conducts electricity', 'hardest natural substance', 'alkane/alkene/alkyne general formula', 'which hydrocarbon is saturated'.
patterns.logic:
1. Allotropes: diamond (hardest, non-conductor), graphite (soft, conducts), fullerene C₆₀, graphene.
2. Families: alkane CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (single bonds, saturated); alkene CₙH₂ₙ (double); alkyne CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (triple).
3. Methane (CH₄) is the simplest alkane and the main gas in CNG/biogas.

example.q: Which general formula belongs to an **alkyne**?
example.solution: **CₙH₂ₙ₋₂** — the triple bond (as in acetylene, C₂H₂) leaves fewer hydrogens than an alkene.

patterns.name: Everyday carbon chemistry
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which alcohol causes blindness', 'vinegar contains…', 'why does soap fail in hard water', 'hydrogenation of oils uses which catalyst', 'esters give…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Alcohols: **methanol = poison (blindness, death)**; ethanol = the alcohol in drinks and petrol blends.
2. Vinegar = 5–8% **acetic acid**; esters (acid + alcohol) = fruity smells.
3. Soap = fatty-acid salt made by **saponification**; forms scum with hard-water Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ — detergents do not.
4. **Hydrogenation** of vegetable oil uses a **nickel catalyst** → vanaspati.

example.q: Soap does not lather well in **hard water** because —
example.solution: Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form insoluble **scum**; synthetic detergents are made to work even so.

patterns.name: Pollutant ↔ disease or event
patterns.howToSpot: 'Minamata disease is caused by…', 'which gas causes acid rain', 'CFCs damage…', 'Bhopal gas tragedy leaked…', 'why is CO poisonous'.
patterns.logic:
1. Japanese diseases: **Minamata–mercury; itai-itai–cadmium**.
2. CO binds **haemoglobin** far more strongly than oxygen → carbon monoxide poisoning.
3. **SO₂ + NOₓ → acid rain**; **CFCs → ozone-hole** (Montreal Protocol 1987); Bhopal 1984 leaked **methyl isocyanate (MIC)**.
4. Greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄ — Kyoto 1997, Paris 2015.

example.q: **Minamata disease** resulted from poisoning by —
example.solution: **Mercury** — factory effluent in Japan entered fish, and fish-eating villagers were poisoned. (Cadmium caused itai-itai.)

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Baking soda is chemically…', 'the formula of washing soda / bleaching powder / plaster of Paris', 'which is called oil of vitriol', wrong-pair questions on the common-names table.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hold one master table: baking soda NaHCO₃, washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, caustic soda NaOH, bleaching powder Ca(OCl)Cl, plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O, gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O, quicklime CaO, limestone CaCO₃, plus the vitriols (oil–H₂SO₄, blue–CuSO₄·5H₂O, green–FeSO₄·7H₂O, white–ZnSO₄). In wrong-pair questions, test the Ca-family against the Na-family first.

example.q: Plaster of Paris is chemically:
example.solution: Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O — made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O); it sets back to gypsum with water.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The acid in tamarind / curd / tomato / lemon / ant sting', match-the-column of foods, stings and acids.
pyqPatterns.approach: Kitchen map: vinegar–acetic, lemon/orange–citric, tamarind and grapes–tartaric, tomato and spinach–oxalic, curd–lactic, apple–malic, ant sting and nettle–formic, stomach–HCl. Traps to kill: tamarind is tartaric (not citric), tomato is oxalic.

example.q: The acid present in an ant sting is:
example.solution: Formic (methanoic) acid — neutralised by rubbing a mild base such as baking soda.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Phenolphthalein is colourless in…', 'turmeric turns…with a base', 'the pH of blood / the tooth-decay threshold', 'solution of pH 4 vs pH 6 — which is more acidic'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Colours: litmus blue→red in acid; phenolphthalein colourless in acid, pink in base; methyl orange red in acid, yellow in base; turmeric reddish-brown in base. pH ladder: gastric ≈ 1–2, lemon ≈ 2, water 7, blood ≈ 7.4, tooth decay < 5.5, acid rain < 5.6; each unit is a ten-fold change.

example.q: Phenolphthalein gives which colour in a basic solution?
example.solution: Pink — it is colourless in acids. 'Pink in Base' is the pair to remember.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Bauxite / cinnabar / galena / pitchblende is the ore of…', 'brass / bronze / solder / stainless steel is an alloy of…', 'which alloy contains tin'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Two lists. Ores: bauxite–Al, haematite–Fe, cinnabar–Hg, galena–Pb, zinc blende–Zn, cassiterite–Sn, copper pyrites–Cu, pitchblende–U, rock salt–Na. Alloys: brass Cu+Zn, bronze Cu+Sn, solder Pb+Sn, stainless Fe+Cr+Ni, duralumin Al+Cu, nichrome Ni+Cr, amalgam metal+Hg. The classic trap is brass–Zn vs bronze–Sn.

example.q: Brass is an alloy of:
example.solution: Copper and zinc. Bronze is the copper–tin alloy — the most common wrong option.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who is the father of the periodic table', 'which is the lightest / most abundant element', symbols from Latin names, element by group (alkali, halogen, noble gas), modern vs Mendeleev.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor facts: Mendeleev–periodic table (by atomic weight), Moseley–modern (by atomic number), Newlands–octaves, Doberiener–triads; H lightest, He most abundant in the universe, O most abundant in the earth's crust, Fe most abundant metal in the crust; Na from natrium, K from kalium, Au from aurum, Fe from ferrum; Group 1 alkali, 17 halogen, 18 noble gases; 7 periods, 18 groups.

example.q: The chemical symbol of sodium, from its Latin name, is:
example.solution: Na (natrium). Potassium is K (kalium), gold Au (aurum), iron Fe (ferrum).

pyqPatterns.pattern: Industrial process, polymer or fuel component
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The Haber process gives…', 'CNG / LPG / biogas mainly contains…', 'first synthetic fibre / first plastic', 'vulcanisation is done with…', 'which process makes sulphuric acid'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Processes: Haber–NH₃, Contact–H₂SO₄, Ostwald–HNO₃, Solvay–Na₂CO₃. Fuels: CNG and biogas–methane, LPG–butane (ethyl mercaptan for smell), welding–acetylene, best coal–anthracite. Polymers: nylon first synthetic fibre, bakelite first plastic, Teflon non-stick, PVC pipes, vulcanisation = rubber + sulphur.

example.q: The Solvay process is used to manufacture:
example.solution: Sodium carbonate (washing soda). Haber gives ammonia, Contact gives sulphuric acid, Ostwald gives nitric acid.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Minamata disease is caused by…', 'the Bhopal gas tragedy leaked…', 'which gas causes acid rain', 'CFCs deplete…', 'why is carbon monoxide poisonous'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pairs: Minamata–mercury, itai-itai–cadmium (both Japan); Bhopal 1984–methyl isocyanate; acid rain–SO₂ + NOₓ; ozone hole–CFCs (Montreal Protocol 1987); CO binds haemoglobin ~200× more strongly than oxygen; greenhouse gases CO₂/CH₄ (Kyoto 1997, Paris 2015).

example.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning with:
example.solution: Mercury — contaminated fish in Minamata Bay, Japan. Cadmium is the itai-itai culprit.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who discovered the electron / proton / neutron', 'the number of electrons in an atom equals…', 'isotopes differ in…', 'maximum electrons in a shell', 'which radiation is charged'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Discoverers: electron–J.J. Thomson, proton–Goldstein, neutron–Chadwick, nucleus–Rutherford, planetary model–Bohr. Identity rules: atomic number Z = protons = electrons; mass number A = protons + neutrons; isotopes differ in neutrons, isobars in mass number. Shell n holds 2n² (2, 8, 18, 32). Cathode rays = electrons; α-particles are positive, β negative, γ neutral.

example.q: Isotopes of an element differ in the number of:
example.solution: Neutrons — same protons (so same element), different mass numbers. Isobars instead share the mass number.

solvedExamples.q: What is the chemical formula of Plaster of Paris?
solvedExamples.solution: **Plaster of Paris** is calcium sulphate **hemihydrate**, CaSO₄·½H₂O, made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) to about 373 K. On mixing with water it sets back into gypsum. CaCO₃ is limestone and CaOCl₂ is bleaching powder.

solvedExamples.q: What is the percentage of pure gold in 22-carat gold (approximately)?
solvedExamples.solution: 24 carat is pure gold, so 22 carat = 22/24 × 100 = **91.67%**. The rest is usually copper or silver for hardness.

solvedExamples.q: Which gas leaked in the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984?
solvedExamples.solution: On the night of 2–3 December 1984, **methyl isocyanate (MIC)** leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, causing one of the world's worst industrial disasters.
**Brass = copper + zinc.** Copper + tin is **bronze**, and lead + tin is **solder**.

practice.q: The chemical name of baking soda is:
practice.solution: Baking soda is **sodium hydrogen carbonate (sodium bicarbonate), NaHCO₃**. Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) is washing soda, and sodium hydroxide is caustic soda.

practice.q: Which acid is present in tamarind?
practice.solution: Tamarind contains **tartaric acid**. Citrus fruits have citric acid, tomato has oxalic acid and curd has lactic acid.

practice.q: The pH of human blood is approximately:
practice.solution: Human blood is **slightly basic, about pH 7.4** (normal range about 7.35–7.45), kept steady by buffer systems.

practice.q: What colour does phenolphthalein show in a basic solution?
practice.solution: Phenolphthalein is **colourless in acidic and neutral** solutions and turns **pink in basic** solutions.

practice.q: Bauxite is the chief ore of:
practice.solution: **Bauxite** (hydrated aluminium oxide) is the chief ore of **aluminium**, extracted by electrolysis (Hall–Héroult process).

practice.q: Solder, used for joining electrical wires, is an alloy of:
practice.solution: **Solder = lead + tin.** Its low melting point lets it melt easily and join wires. Copper + zinc is brass, copper + tin is bronze.

practice.q: Which metal is stored under kerosene to prevent it from reacting with air and moisture?
practice.solution: **Sodium** (and potassium) react vigorously with oxygen and water — sodium can catch fire — so they are kept **under kerosene**. White phosphorus, a non-metal, is stored under water.

practice.q: Which metal is a liquid at normal room temperature?
practice.solution: **Mercury** is the metal that is liquid at room temperature. **Bromine** is also liquid but is a **non-metal**. Gallium melts at about 30 °C — in the palm — but is solid at a normal room temperature of about 25 °C.
practice.shortcut: Liquid metal = Hg; liquid non-metal = Br.

practice.q: The modern periodic table is based on:
practice.solution: Henry **Moseley** showed that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their **atomic number**, which is the basis of the modern periodic law. Mendeleev's table was based on atomic mass.

practice.q: Isotopes of an element have the same:
practice.solution: **Isotopes** have the **same atomic number** (protons) but **different mass numbers** because their neutron counts differ. Their chemical properties are similar; physical properties such as density differ.

practice.q: Which of the following substances undergoes sublimation?
practice.solution: **Camphor** changes directly from solid to vapour — **sublimation**. Naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice also sublime.

practice.q: The Haber process is used for the manufacture of:
practice.solution: The **Haber process** combines nitrogen and hydrogen over an **iron catalyst** to make **ammonia**. Sulphuric acid comes from the Contact process, nitric acid from the Ostwald process and sodium carbonate from the Solvay process.

practice.q: Teflon, used in non-stick cookware, is a polymer of:
practice.solution: **Teflon** is polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), made from **tetrafluoroethylene**. Vinyl chloride gives PVC, isoprene gives natural rubber and ethene gives polythene.

practice.q: The main constituent of CNG (compressed natural gas) is:
practice.solution: CNG is mostly **methane**. LPG is mainly **butane** with propane.

practice.q: Minamata disease is caused by poisoning from:
practice.solution: **Minamata disease** (Japan, 1950s) was caused by **methylmercury** in industrial wastewater, which accumulated in fish. Cadmium caused itai-itai disease.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **chemical** change?
practice.solution: Rusting forms a **new substance (iron oxide)** and cannot be reversed by simple means. Melting, dissolving and boiling change only the form — physical changes.

practice.q: **Dry ice** is —
practice.solution: **Dry ice** is solid CO₂, which sublimes directly into gas — used for cooling and stage effects.

practice.q: Which of the following does **NOT** sublime?
practice.solution: The sublimation set is **camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice**. Common salt stays solid and is separated from camphor exactly by sublimation.

practice.q: **Cream is separated from milk** by —
practice.solution: Spinning in a **centrifuge** throws the denser skimmed milk outward and collects the lighter cream at the centre.

practice.q: **Dyes in ink** can be separated by —
practice.solution: In **chromatography** the dye parts travel different distances up the paper because they dissolve and stick differently — used to separate dyes, pigments and drugs.

practice.q: A **mixture of salt and camphor** is separated by —
practice.solution: Camphor **sublimes** on heating and its vapour condenses on a cold surface, leaving salt behind.

practice.q: **Milk** is an example of —
practice.solution: Milk is liquid fat droplets dispersed in water — an **emulsion** (liquid in liquid). Fog is an aerosol; smoke is solid in gas.

practice.q: The **scattering of a beam of light** by colloidal particles is called the —
practice.solution: The **Tyndall effect** makes the beam's path visible in fog or a colloidal solution. **Brownian motion** is the zig-zag jitter of the particles themselves.

practice.q: The **plum-pudding model** of the atom was proposed by —
practice.solution: After discovering the electron, **Thomson** imagined electrons embedded in a positive sphere like plums in a pudding. Rutherford later replaced it with the nuclear model.

practice.q: The correct historical **order of atomic models** is —
practice.solution: Dalton's indivisible atoms (1803), Thomson's electron model (1897), Rutherford's nuclear model (1911), Bohr's orbits (1913).

practice.q: Atoms of the same element with **different mass numbers** are called —
practice.solution: **Isotopes** share the atomic number Z but differ in neutrons (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars share the mass number A instead.

practice.q: The average atomic mass of chlorine (³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl) is about **35.5** because —
options: The two isotopes occur in the ratio 3 : 1
practice.solution: ³⁵Cl is about three times as abundant as ³⁷Cl, so the weighted average works out near **35.5**.

practice.q: Calcium has atomic number **20**. The electron arrangement **2, 8, 8, 2** means its M shell holds —
practice.solution: Filling order: K = 2, L = 8, then M begins; for calcium it stops at **8** before the N shell takes the last 2. (The M shell's maximum by 2n² is 18, but the actual count here is 8.)

practice.q: How many **moles** are there in **36 g of water**? (H₂O = 18 g/mol)
practice.solution: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 36 ÷ 18 = **2 moles**.

practice.q: A gas fills **600 mL at 1 atm**. At constant temperature, the pressure needed to compress it to **400 mL** is —
practice.solution: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → 1 × 600 = P₂ × 400 → P₂ = **1.5 atm**. (0.67 atm comes from dividing the wrong way.)

practice.q: A gas occupies **300 mL at 27 °C**. Keeping the pressure constant, its volume at **127 °C** will be —
practice.solution: Charles's law needs **kelvin**: 27 °C = 300 K, 127 °C = 400 K. V₂ = 300 × 400/300 = **400 mL**. Using Celsius directly is the standard error.

practice.q: The most abundant element in the **Earth's crust** is —
practice.solution: Crust order: **O > Si > Al > Fe > Ca** (mnemonic OSAIC). Oxygen is about 46% by mass.

practice.q: The **lightest metal** is —
practice.solution: **Lithium** (group 1) is the lightest of all metals — even it floats on oil. Hydrogen is lighter still, but it is not a metal.

practice.q: Which is the only **liquid non-metal** at room temperature?
practice.solution: **Bromine** is a fuming red-brown liquid. Mercury is the liquid *metal*; chlorine is a gas; iodine is a solid.

practice.q: The metal with the **highest melting point**, used as a bulb filament, is —
practice.solution: **Tungsten (W)** melts at about 3400 °C — the highest of all metals — so a white-hot filament survives. Its symbol comes from wolfram.

practice.q: The most abundant **metal in the human body** is —
practice.solution: **Calcium** (bones and teeth) tops the body's metal list; iron is the most abundant trace metal. Oxygen is the most abundant element overall.

practice.q: The chemical symbol of **potassium** is —
practice.solution: From Latin **kalium**. P is phosphorus, Po polonium, Pt platinum.

practice.q: Which symbol comes from the Latin word **plumbum**?
practice.solution: **Plumbum** = lead (Pb) — the same root gives 'plumber'.

practice.q: The **law of octaves** was proposed by —
practice.solution: **Newlands** arranged 56 elements by mass and found every 8th element similar — like octaves in music. Döbereiner had earlier found triads.

practice.q: Mendeleev's periodic table was based on —
practice.solution: **Mendeleev** used atomic mass and even left gaps for unknown elements. The modern table (after Moseley) uses **atomic number** instead.

practice.q: The **modern periodic law** states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their —
practice.solution: **Moseley** showed atomic number (protons) — not mass — decides periodicity, fixing the anomalies of Mendeleev's table.

practice.q: The modern periodic table has —
practice.solution: **18 vertical groups, 7 horizontal periods**, with 118 elements named so far.

practice.q: On moving **left to right across a period**, atomic size —
practice.solution: Nuclear charge rises while shells stay the same, pulling electrons closer — so atoms **shrink** across a period and metallic character falls.

practice.q: The elements of **group 17** are called —
practice.solution: **Halogens** (F, Cl, Br, I) — 'salt-formers'. Group 1 alkali metals, group 18 noble gases.

practice.q: Which pair of elements belongs to the **same group** of the periodic table?
practice.solution: Li, Na and K all sit in **group 1** (alkali metals) — one outer electron each, all soft and reactive, stored under oil or kerosene.

practice.q: The chemical name of **baking soda** is —
practice.solution: Baking soda = **sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃)** — a mild, non-poisonous base used in food and as an antacid.

practice.q: **Caustic soda** is —
practice.solution: **Caustic soda** = sodium hydroxide (NaOH), made with chlorine and hydrogen by electrolysis of brine. KOH is caustic potash.

practice.q: **Plaster of Paris** is chemically —
practice.solution: Plaster of Paris is **calcium sulphate hemihydrate**, made by heating gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O); with water it sets back to hard gypsum.

practice.q: **Bleaching powder** is chemically —
practice.solution: **Ca(OCl)Cl** — calcium oxychloride — disinfects drinking water and bleaches cotton.

practice.q: The acid present in **lemon** is —
practice.solution: Lemon and orange give **citric acid**. Vinegar–acetic; tamarind–tartaric; curd–lactic.

practice.q: An **ant sting** hurts because it injects —
options: Lactic acid, which lime water neutralises
Formic acid, which baking soda neutralises
practice.solution: The sting injects **formic (methanoic) acid**; rubbing baking soda (a mild base) neutralises it. A wasp sting is alkaline — vinegar is used there instead.

practice.q: **Oxalic acid** is found in —
practice.solution: **Oxalic acid** — tomato and spinach. Curd has lactic acid; vinegar acetic; apple malic.

practice.q: **Phenolphthalein** turns —
practice.solution: Phenolphthalein is **colourless in acid and pink in base** — the classic 'Pink in Base' pair.

practice.q: The pH of **human blood** is about —
practice.solution: Blood is kept between 7.35 and 7.45 — **slightly basic**. 5.5 is the tooth-decay threshold; 9 is like milk of magnesia.

practice.q: **Tooth decay** begins when the pH of the mouth falls below about —
practice.solution: Below **pH 5.5** mouth acids (made by bacteria from sugar) start dissolving tooth enamel — the standard exam value.

practice.q: The pH of a solution changes from **4 to 2**. Its hydrogen-ion concentration —
practice.solution: Each pH unit is a **ten-fold** change in H⁺; two units means 10 × 10 = 100 times more acidic.

practice.q: **Carbon dioxide** passed through lime water turns it —
practice.solution: CO₂ reacts with dissolved Ca(OH)₂ to form insoluble **calcium carbonate** — a white milky precipitate. This is the standard test for CO₂.

practice.q: The **chlor-alkali process** (electrolysis of brine) produces —
options: Washing soda and bleaching powder only
practice.solution: Electrolysing concentrated brine gives **caustic soda at the cathode, chlorine at the anode and hydrogen** — the 'chlor-alkali' trio.

practice.q: Adding water to **quicklime (CaO)** gives —
options: Slaked lime with much heat released
practice.solution: CaO + H₂O → **Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime)** + heat — an exothermic combination used in whitewashing.

practice.q: **Permanent hardness** of water is removed by —
practice.solution: **Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O)** precipitates the Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions that cause permanent hardness. Boiling only removes temporary (bicarbonate) hardness.

practice.q: Cakes and idli batter turn **fluffy** because baking soda —
options: Releases CO₂ on heating with an acid
practice.solution: NaHCO₃ + acid (or heat) gives **CO₂ bubbles** that puff up the dough. The same reaction pressurises soda-acid fire extinguishers.

practice.q: **Oil of vitriol** is the old name for —
practice.solution: **H₂SO₄** — called oil of vitriol. Blue vitriol is CuSO₄·5H₂O, green vitriol FeSO₄·7H₂O, white vitriol ZnSO₄.

practice.q: When **blue copper sulphate crystals** are heated strongly, they —
options: Turn white as water of crystallisation is lost
practice.solution: Heating drives off the 5H₂O; the anhydrous CuSO₄ left behind is **white** — and turns blue again if moistened.

practice.q: **Bauxite** is the chief ore of —
practice.solution: **Bauxite** (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) gives aluminium; iron comes from haematite and magnetite.

practice.q: **Galena** is the principal ore of —
practice.solution: **Galena (PbS)** is lead sulphide. Cinnabar is mercury's ore; cassiterite, tin's.

practice.q: **Pitchblende** is an important ore of —
practice.solution: **Pitchblende** is uranium oxide (U₃O₈) — the Curies processed tonnes of it to find radium.

practice.q: **Brass** is an alloy of —
practice.solution: **Brass = Cu + Zn**; bronze = Cu + Sn. Both look golden, but the second metal differs.

practice.q: **Solder**, used for joining wires, is an alloy of —
practice.solution: **Solder (Pb + Sn)** has a low melting point, so it melts and flows around the joint easily.

practice.q: **Stainless steel** resists corrosion mainly because of the added —
practice.solution: Stainless steel = **iron + chromium (about 10–20%) + nickel** (+ carbon). The chromium forms a protective oxide skin.
